definition: The systematic weakness of benchmarks outside English: fewer native test sets, contamination via translation, and cultural misalignment of translated benchmarks.
details: The systematic weakness of benchmarks outside English: fewer native test sets, contamination via translation, and cultural misalignment of translated benchmarks. Arabic-specific suites (native-authored MMLU-style sets, dialect benchmarks) exist precisely because translated evals overstate real capability.

explainer.lead: Benchmarks outside English are systematically weaker, with fewer native test sets, contamination from translation and cultural mismatch. It matters because translated evals can overstate real capability in other languages.

tiers.eli5: A test translated from another country may ask about things you never learned, so a good score does not prove you truly know the subject.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers building non-English systems need native-authored test sets, since translated benchmarks leak through training data and misjudge culturally specific tasks. A pitfall is trusting a translated score as evidence of local capability.
tiers.paperLevel: The gap arises from three sources: sparse native test sets, contamination when translations overlap pretraining data, and cultural misalignment of translated items. Limits: no single standard correction; native suites are needed per language.

explainer.example: An Arabic MMLU-style set authored natively by Arabic speakers reveals lower scores than a translated English benchmark, showing the translated score overstated capability.
